lines: You were born with a small companion.
It was there before you could speak. It kept you from the edge of the stairs. From the hot stove. From the deep end of the water.
At night, when there was a noise in the dark, it was the one who woke you.
Its name is fear. And it has loved you, in its clumsy way, every day of your life.
Fear has only one job. To keep you alive.
It is very old. Older than words. It cannot read, and it cannot tell time.
It does not know the difference between a cliff and a job interview. Between a wolf and a hard conversation. It only knows: this might hurt you.
So it tugs at your sleeve. Before you speak up. Before you open the letter. Before you say, I love you.
It is not trying to ruin your life. It is trying to save it. It just does not know what your life is for.
Nobody teaches us what to do with it. So most of us do one of two things.
Some of us obey it. Every time it tugs, we turn back. And our life gets a little smaller. One room at a time.
And some of us fight it. We call it weak. We lock it in the cellar, and pretend it is not there.
But a frightened thing that is ignored does not go quiet. It gets louder. It bangs on the door at three in the morning.
There is a third way. And it is very old.
In a novel called Dune, a boy, alone and in pain, says a kind of prayer.
I will face my fear. I will permit it to pass over me, and through me.
Permit. Not defeat. Not destroy. He lets it come, the way you let weather come. And he stays.
And long before that novel, people said the same thing, in every language they had.
Fear not. Be not afraid. It is in the Hebrew prophets, in the Quran, in the Gospels. In India it became a gesture. One open hand, raised.
But listen to what comes after the words. Almost every time, it is the same. For I am with you.
Nobody ever calmed a frightened child by saying, stop being scared.
You kneel down. You open your arms. You say: I am here.
And here is the quiet secret. You can do that for your own fear.
You can kneel down to it. You can say: I see you. You are trying to protect me. Thank you.
I am here. And we are going anyway.
Fear does not have to leave for you to move. It can come with you. It just cannot drive.
Something softens when you do this. Scientists have watched it happen. When people put a feeling into words, the brain's alarm quiets. When someone they love holds their hand, it quiets more.
The fear was never asking you to stop. It was asking not to be alone.
So you walk through the door together. Into the room. Into the conversation. Into the letter.
And on the other side, something strange happens. Your small companion looks around. And goes quiet.
The boy in the novel knew this too. Where the fear has gone, there will be nothing. Only I will remain.
And the one who remains is a little larger than before. Large enough to hold a frightened thing, and keep walking.
You will never be fearless. You do not need to be.
The next time it tugs at your sleeve, try putting a hand on your chest.
And say, the way you would to a child in the dark: hello, old friend. I know. I am with you.
Fear not.
